Adam.myth: The rulers construct Adam from cosmic substances
Adam.note: They model Adam’s body on a reflected heavenly image but cannot initially make him stand.

Adam.note: Yaldabaoth is tricked into breathing his stolen divine light into Adam.
Azazel is associated with the tempter who leads Adam into transgression.
ʿAzāzīl refuses to bow to Adam, claiming fiery superiority over clay.
Azrael gathers the earth from which Adam’s body is formed.
Later narratives make Azrael attend Adam’s death or extract his soul.
As last or second Adam, Christ reverses the first Adam's failure.
Christ liberates Adam and the other righteous dead from the underworld.
The Manichaean Christ awakens Adam and reveals his divine origin.
Yaldabaoth and his rulers form Adam’s body, and Yaldabaoth’s breath inadvertently transfers divine power.

Iblīs refuses to prostrate before Adam and claims fiery superiority.

Lilith is created as Adam’s wife but abandons him after their sexual dispute.

Sophia’s stolen power enters Adam through Yaldabaoth’s breath and assists his awakening.
Yaldabaoth and his rulers form Adam after the heavenly image.
Yaldabaoth orders his powers to copy the luminous human archetype.
The chief ruler and archons fashion the earthly Adam.
His breath unknowingly transfers higher power into Adam.
Yaldabaoth breathes Sophia's stolen power into Adam, enabling him to rise.
Yaldabaoth encloses Adam in material forgetfulness and imposes paradise's prohibition.

Adam ha-Rishon.note: Earthly Adam is the lower created image or reflection of Adam Kadmon.

Adam’s unnamed spouse.note: Iblīs tempts Adam’s spouse alongside Adam and induces them to eat.

Adonaios.note: Adonaios is one of Yaldabaoth's six named children.
Adonaios.source: On the Origin of the World

Adoneus.note: Adoneus belongs to the descending sevenfold line begun by Ialdabaoth.

Agrat bat Mahlat.note: A competing later Jewish genealogy names Agrat bat Mahlat as Ashmedai's mother.

Akraziel.note: Older compilations equate Raziel with Akraziel through similar offices and exegetical wordplay.

Albion.note: Blake’s universal human is compared structurally with Adam Kadmon, though direct dependence remains debated.

Amiorps.myth: Seven rulers govern demons of bodily members
Amiorps.note: Amiorps and Uriel are named together among seven rulers over bodily demons.

Anafiel.note: Anafiel guards or admits the visionary near Metatron, though their hierarchy varies by recension.

Anakim.note: The spies describe the sons of Anak as descended from or belonging to the Nephilim.

Angel of YHWH.myth: Ahaziah and the oracle of Ekron
Angel of YHWH.note: The angel orders Elijah to intercept the messengers and denounce Baal-zebub’s consultation.
Satan accuses Joshua before the angel, who participates in Joshua’s restoration.

Angels.note: Angels announce, worship, serve, accompany, and are subordinated to Christ.
Jibrīl and the angels collectively support Muḥammad.
Angels scatter burning roses, distract Mephistopheles, and seize Faust's immortal part from him.

Angra Mainyu.note: Modern comparative religion sometimes equates Iblīs with Angra Mainyu.

Antichrist.note: Christ destroys the eschatological opponent at his coming.

Arikh Anpin.myth: Rectification after the breaking of vessels
Arikh Anpin.note: Arikh Anpin emerges as a downstream partzuf in the rectified world below Adam Kadmon.

Armoupieel.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Armoupieel as the tenth authority.

Arʿtaqof.note: Arʿtaqof appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Asmenedas.myth: Seven rulers govern demons of bodily members
Asmenedas.note: Asmenedas and Uriel are named together among seven rulers over bodily demons.

Astanphaeus.note: Astanphaeus completes the descending sevenfold line begun by Ialdabaoth.

Astaphaios.note: Astaphaios is one of Yaldabaoth's six named children.
Astaphaios.source: On the Origin of the World

Astaroth.note: Astaroth and Beelzebub appear together as alleged infernal signatories or witnesses.

Astraios.note: Astraios and Eōs generate the morning star in Greek astral genealogy.

Athoth.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Athoth as the first authority.

Authades.note: Authades deceives Pistis Sophia with false light, drawing her from her appointed region.
Authades persecutes Pistis Sophia through his emanations and steals her light-powers.
Yaldabaoth emanates from and remains subordinate to Authades.
Yaldabaoth joins Authades in persecuting Pistis Sophia and taking her light.

Aēšma.note: Modern scholarship proposes Aēšma as Asmodeus's linguistic-religious antecedent, with conceptual continuity remaining uncertain.

Bahamūt.note: The cosmic fish's name may derive from Behemoth, but their identity is unproven.

Baphomet.note: Modern occult art sometimes equates Abraxas with Baphomet without ancient or medieval support.
Modern occult imagery and LaVeyan symbolism made Baphomet Satanic despite distinct origins.
Modern reception often identifies Lévi’s Baphomet image with Satan.

Bar Yokhni.note: Medieval commentators and Ginzberg conflate Ziz with the egg-laying giant bird.

Barachiel.myth: Collective commemoration of the chief archangels
Barachiel.note: Uriel and Barachiel appear jointly in Eastern Orthodox synaxes and icons.

Barakiel.myth: Angels bring souls from darkness to judgment
Barakiel.note: Uriel and Barakiel jointly bring human souls before God’s judgment.

Baraqʾel.note: Baraqʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Bashīr.note: Later theologians identify or replace the righteous believer’s questioners with Bashīr and Mubashshir.

Beelzeboul.note: Later translations and modern occult syntheses sometimes call Beelzeboul a jinn.

Belias.note: Yaldabaoth generates Belias, the twelfth authority stationed over Hades.

Belphegor.note: Belphegor governs gluttony while Mammon governs avarice; they share no narrative episode.

Berith.note: Berith purportedly reveals a hierarchy placing Beelzebub near Lucifer.

Biblical serpent.note: Mephistopheles jokingly calls the serpent his aunt; the remark is not literal genealogy.

Bileth.note: Bileth ranks first and Belial second among the imprisoned spirit-kings.

Binah.note: The lower Shekhinah is portrayed as Binah’s reflection within upper-lower Shekhinah schemes.
Modern comparative and esoteric writings sometimes equate Binah with Sophia.

Cain.note: Yaldabaoth generates the cosmic Cain and appoints him sixth authority.

Cephalus.note: Hyginian mythography associates Eōsphoros genealogically with Eōs and Cephalus.

Ceyx.note: Ovid calls Ceyx the son of Lucifer, though Lucifer takes no active role.

Cherub.note: A cherub gives Gabriel fire, which Gabriel casts upon Jerusalem.

Chnoubis.note: Some scholars identify or connect particular lion-serpent gems with Yaldabaoth.

Christian Holy Spirit.note: Later Christian interpretations identify both with divine presence or a feminine aspect of divinity.

Daniʾel.note: Daniʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Daveithe.note: Abrasax and Daveithe occur within the same ministerial celestial hierarchy.
Daveithe.source: Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit

Death.note: Death and personified Abaddon jointly report hearing only rumors of Wisdom.

Christ reigns until the personified power Death is finally destroyed.
Michael conveys God's commands while personified Death finally brings about Abraham's death.
Satan fathers Death upon Sin in Milton’s allegorical genealogy.
Death confronts Satan until Sin intervenes between them.

Death.myth: Final judgment in the lake of fire
Death.note: Satan and personified Death are separately consigned to the lake of fire.
Milton makes Death the offspring of Satan and Sin.
Yaldabaoth produces Death, which generates further destructive powers.
Death.source: On the Origin of the World

Demons.note: Powers, Michael, and other armed angels restrain or defeat demons.

Dhū al-Janāḥ.note: Modern posters place both sacred mounts together without narrating a meeting.

Divine Voice.myth: Rabbah bar bar Hana's sea voyage

Dumah.note: Metatron receives accounts concerning the dead from Dumah and presents them before his Master.

Earlier prophets collectively.note: Earlier prophets are said to have ridden Burāq.
Burāq is tethered at the Jerusalem ring used by prophets.

Earth.note: The future Angel of Death takes soil despite Earth’s plea and receives the death office.
Azrael takes clay despite Earth invoking God’s protection.

Ein Sof.note: Ein Sof’s ray forms or fills Adam Kadmon after tzimtzum.

Elaios.note: Elaios is one of Yaldabaoth's six named children.
Elaios.source: On the Origin of the World

Elect One.note: Michael stands among the heavenly presences attending judgment associated with the Elect One.

Elijah.note: Elijah appears and converses with Christ during the transfiguration.

Elimi.note: Elimi and Beelzebub appear together as alleged infernal signatories or witnesses.

Eloeus.note: Eloeus belongs to the descending sevenfold line begun by Ialdabaoth.

Empusa.note: Mephistopheles pursues and is mocked or deceived by the classical female monster.

Enoch.note: Enoch tells Asael and the Watchers that their petition is denied.

Enoch.myth: Metatron reveals his former human identity
Enoch.note: Metatron tells Rabbi Ishmael that he is Enoch son of Jared.

Ephippas.note: Ephippas appears in Beelzeboul’s command narrative, with their hierarchy varying by recension.

Eternal Life.note: Eternal Life appears at Barbelo’s request within the divine pentad.

Eve.myth: The rulers pursue and assault the spiritual Woman

Christ liberates Eve with Adam and the righteous dead from the underworld.
Plaskow’s intentionally new midrash makes Lilith return to Eden and form solidarity with Eve.
Yaldabaoth and the rulers participate in producing or pursuing the female figure.

Ialdabaoth's economy opposes Eve's awakening and seeks control of spiritual power.

Ezrael.note: The Ethiopic punisher probably adapts the Islamicate death angel rather than representing an independent being.

First Beast from the sea.myth: The dragon empowers the sea beast
First Beast from the sea.note: The dragon gives the beast his power, throne, and authority.

Foreknowledge.note: Foreknowledge stands with Thought-Barbelo and glorifies the Invisible Spirit.

Gallizur.note: Older compilations equate Raziel with Gallizur through similar revelatory functions and wordplay.

Gamaliel.note: Abrasax and Gamaliel appear as fellow celestial ministers.

Gamaliel.note: Abrasax and Gamaliel descend together in luminous clouds and rescue the imperishable people.

Gello.note: Later folklore sometimes merges Lilith with the Mediterranean child-killing demon Gello or Gyllou.

Giant offspring.note: Gabriel causes the violent giant offspring of the Watchers to destroy one another.

God / the Holy One.myth: God sends Raziel to convey a sacred book to Adam
God / the Holy One.note: God commissions Raziel to transmit heavenly secrets and sacred knowledge to Adam.

God / the Holy One.myth: Raziel transmits divine authority through the book

God of the Jews.note: The Jewish God is portrayed as a contentious world-making angel subordinate to Abraxas.

God the Father.note: Milton’s loyal seraphim uphold and serve the Father’s heavenly monarchy.

God's angels.note: The Greek translation says Behemoth was made for God's angels to play with.

Great Nous.note: Jesus the Splendor represents or embodies the Manichaean saving Mind.

Guyon.myth: Guyon's trial in the Cave of Mammon
Guyon.note: Mammon tempts Guyon with gold, advancement, and Philotime's hand; Guyon refuses.

Harmas.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Harmas as the second authority.

Hermoni.note: Hermoni appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Homunculus.note: Homunculus recognizes Mephistopheles and travels with him and Faust toward the classical realm.

Hormin.note: Some manuscripts call the prodigious Hormin a son of Lilith.

Hārūn.note: Aaron appears in the ascent complex without direct Burāq interaction.

Iao.note: Ialdabaoth generates Iao as the next ruler in the chain.

Ibrāhīm.note: Burāq is said to carry Abraham on visits to Mecca.

Idrīs.note: Idrīs appears in the ascent complex without direct Burāq interaction.

Iggeret daughter of Mahalath.note: Iggeret is named with Lilith and Naamah among surviving unclean spirits.

Imma.myth: Rectification after the breaking of vessels
Imma.note: Imma emerges as a downstream partzuf in the rectified world below Adam Kadmon.

Incorruptibility.note: Incorruptibility appears at Barbelo’s request and joins the pleromic praise.

Ismāʿīl.note: Ishmael receives Abraham’s visits made by Burāq, without direct interaction.

Istehar.note: Shemhazai attempts to obtain Istehar by revealing the divine Name she demands.

Jacob-Israel.myth: Uriel wrestles the incarnate archangel Israel

Jehudiel.myth: Collective commemoration of the chief archangels
Jehudiel.note: Uriel and Jehudiel appear jointly in Eastern Orthodox synaxes and icons.

Jeremiel.note: Jeremiel answers waiting souls within the same apocalypse interpreted chiefly by Uriel.

Jeremiel.myth: Collective commemoration of the chief archangels
Jeremiel.note: Some Eastern Orthodox lists commemorate Jeremiel jointly with Uriel.

Jesus.note: Archontic Death is overcome or dissolved by revelation and the Savior.

Jesus.myth: Ialdabaoth unknowingly prepares conditions for Jesus
Jesus.note: Ialdabaoth unknowingly helps prepare the circumstances for Jesus within the lower creation.

Jonah.note: Jonah displays Abraham’s covenantal seal and causes Leviathan to flee.

Kalila-Oumbri.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Kalila-Oumbri as the third authority.

Kokabʾel.note: Kokabʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Lumiel.note: Montalban's angelic magical system often identifies Lumiel with Lucifer.

Matarʾel.note: Matarʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Melchizedek.note: Melchizedek judges Belial and the spirits belonging to his lot.

Mubashshir.note: Later theologians identify or replace the righteous believer’s questioners with Mubashshir and Bashīr.

Nuqva.myth: Rectification after the breaking of vessels

Oberon.note: Mephistopheles appears within or beside the pageant celebrating Oberon's golden wedding.

Ofanniel.note: They are placed under Ofanniel, their appointed celestial prince.

Oraios.note: Oraios is one of Yaldabaoth's six named children.

Oreus.note: Oreus belongs to the descending sevenfold line begun by Ialdabaoth.

Peacock.note: Later stories say Iblīs deceives the peacock into aiding his entry.

Pistis Sophia.myth: Pistis Sophia generates or expels the arrogant ruler

Pistis Sophia.myth: Pistis Sophia passes through lower cosmic punishments

Pistis Sophia.myth: Reorganization of the lower archonic order
Pistis Sophia.note: Her action exposes or reorganizes the lower hierarchy of archons and angels.

Pistis Sophia.note: Pistis Sophia precipitates the boastful blind ruler into chaos.

Pistis Sophia.note: Pistis rebukes his boast and proclaims the immortal human above him.

Pistis Sophia.note: Yaldabaoth joins Authades in persecuting Pistis Sophia and taking her light.

Power.note: Power emanates within the hypostatic chain whose first source is Abraxas.

Protennoia.note: Protennoia enters his cosmos and rescues those belonging to the light.

Protophanes.note: Protophanes is a first-appearing level within the articulated Barbelo aeon.

Providence.note: Providence belongs to the chain of hypostases originating from Abraxas.

Puruṣa.note: Theosophy correlated Adam Kadmon with Puruṣa; medieval Kabbalah does not support this identity.

Rahab.myth: Rahab retrieves Raziel’s book from the sea

Ramiel.myth: Angels bring souls from darkness to judgment

Raʿmaʾel.note: Raʿmaʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Remaʾel.note: Remaʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Renanim.note: Ginzberg identifies Ziz with Renanim, derived from Job's conspicuous bird.

Richram.myth: Seven rulers govern demons of bodily members
Richram.note: Richram and Uriel are named together among seven rulers over bodily demons.

Rikbiel.note: They fall within or overlap Rikbiel’s jurisdiction over the chariot wheels.

Riḍwān.note: Riḍwān sometimes appears beside Burāq in expanded Paradise tours.

Rumi.note: Azrael appears as a beautiful visitor whom the dying saint willingly welcomes.

Rūmān.note: Weak late reports place Rūmān in the grave before Munkar and Nakir.

Sablo.note: Abrasax and Sablo jointly lift the imperishable people beyond the hostile rulers.

Sahariʾel.note: Sahariʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Sakla.note: Abrasax rescues people attacked within Sakla's lower dominion without directly fighting Sakla.

Sansenoy.note: Sansenoy pursues Lilith, threatens her offspring, and receives her amuletic oath.

Saphasatoel.myth: Seven rulers govern demons of bodily members
Saphasatoel.note: Saphasatoel and Uriel are named together among seven rulers over bodily demons.

Satanael.note: The Slavonic recension substitutes Satanael for Greek Samael as the planter.

Satanail.note: Some recensions associate the rebellious Grigori with Satanail.

Satoʾel.note: Satoʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Sekwi.note: Later harmonizing accounts identify Ziz with Job's perceptive creature Sekwi.

Selaphiel.myth: Collective commemoration of the chief archangels

Semangelof.note: Semangelof pursues Lilith, threatens her offspring, and receives her amuletic oath.

Serpent.note: Later stories make the serpent carry Iblīs into paradise.

Shamshiʾel.note: Shamshiʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Soul.note: Plotinus treats Soul as an eternal productive and ordering agency within the demiurgic hierarchy.

Sphinxes.note: Mephistopheles questions and banters with the Sphinxes while disoriented in the classical landscape.

Stars of El.note: Hêlēl proposes to raise his throne above the divine stars.

The Elect One.note: They join the heavenly powers assembled in his eschatological court.

The Lord.note: Wisdom proceeds from his mouth and receives Israel and Jerusalem as her dwelling.

Theletos.note: Theletos is Sophia’s male partner in the Valentinian aeonic syzygy.
Sophia attempts knowledge or generation without her male syzygy Theletos.

Theotokos.note: Later Orthodox iconography and Sophiology present Mary as bearing or manifesting Sophia.

Thrones.note: Later Christian interpretation equates Ezekiel’s wheels with the angelic order of Thrones.

Tiferet.myth: Sabbath union of Malkhut and Tiferet
Tiferet.note: Tiferet is her bridegroom; sin separates them and commandments restore their union.

Titania.note: Mephistopheles appears within or beside the pageant celebrating Titania's golden wedding.

Tumiʾel.note: Tumiʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Turiʾel.note: Turiʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Urizen.note: Modern interpretation compares Blake’s oppressive world-forming lawgiver with the Demiurge without claiming historical identity.
Urizen.source: Blake, The First Book of Urizen

Vesper.note: Lucifer and Vesper are distinct morning and evening appearances of one planet.

Virgin Mary.note: Michael escorts or protects Mary's soul and body in later Dormition and Assumption traditions.

Virgin of Light.note: The Virgin of Light is closely associated with Jesus the Splendor.

Will-o’-the-Wisp.note: Mephistopheles commands the spirit to guide him and Faust toward the Brocken.

Woland.note: Bulgakov's demonic cat Behemoth serves as a member of Woland's entourage.

YHWH.myth: Ahaziah and the oracle of Ekron
YHWH.note: Baal-zebub’s foreign oracle is opposed to YHWH’s authority through Elijah.
YHWH speaks between the Ark cherubim and is enthroned above them.
A cherub carries YHWH through a storm-theophany as his flying mount.
The glory mounts above the cherubim and departs the polluted Temple with them.

YHWH.myth: Mobile throne vision and departure from Jerusalem
YHWH.note: They accompany and carry the divine glory as it moves and departs.
They attend his throne, proclaim his holiness, and purify from his altar.
The Shekhinah is YHWH’s dwelling and manifest presence.

YHWH.myth: Separation and reunion of the Bride and Holy King
YHWH.note: The feminine Shekhinah separates from and reunites with the Holy King.
YHWH acquires, creates, establishes, or brings forth Wisdom before creation.
Biblical covenants, lawgiving, and divine sayings are reassigned to Ialdabaoth.

Yabel.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Yabel as the fourth authority.

Yahoel.note: Yahoel identifies, rebukes, and drives away Azazel’s unclean bird form.

Yamm/Sea.note: Lotan belongs to Yamm’s complex, perhaps as servant, ally, or manifestation.

Yao.note: Yao is one of Yaldabaoth's six named children.
Yao.source: On the Origin of the World

Yaḥyā.note: John appears in the ascent complex without direct Burāq interaction.

Yehadiʾel.note: Yehadiʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Yesod.myth: Transmission of generative influx into Malkhut
Yesod.note: Yesod channels masculine generative influx into Shekhinah in a frequently sexualized relationship.

Yobel.note: Yaldabaoth generates and appoints Yobel as the ninth authority.

Yomiʾel.note: Yomiʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Youel.note: Youel’s instruction guides visionaries toward knowledge and contemplation of the Barbelo aeon.

Younger Lilith.note: Kabbalistic demonology pairs Asmodeus with the younger Lilith as his consort.

Yūsuf.note: Joseph appears in the ascent complex without direct Burāq interaction.

Zamael.note: Western occult tables variously conflate or distinguish these martial angelic names from Samael.

Zeqʾel.note: Zeqʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

Zeʿir Anpin.myth: Rectification after the breaking of vessels
Zeʿir Anpin.note: Zeʿir Anpin emerges as a downstream partzuf in the rectified world below Adam Kadmon.

al-Jānn.note: Later exegetes make al-Jānn the primordial father of the jinn.

angels.note: Later prophetic tales say angels defeated corrupt, warring jinn on earth.

demonic children.note: Lilith has demonic offspring, one hundred of whom are condemned to die daily.

dīv.note: Islamicate Persian translation and folklore sometimes equate jinn with dīv.

elder Lilith.note: Some kabbalistic schemes place Asmodeus beneath or alongside the elder Lilith's royal pair.

evil spirits.note: After the giants die, spirits proceeding from their hybrid bodies become destructive earthly spirits.

fallen angels.note: Medieval synthesis makes Lucifer leader and instigator of the angels joining his revolt.

female Leviathan.note: The male and female form a primordial pair whose reproduction would destroy the world.

ghūl.note: Medieval cosmographers and folklorists increasingly classify the ghūl among jinn.

giants.note: Named archangels execute divine judgments against the giants fathered by Watchers.

holy living creatures.note: They produce fire and praise together with the holy living creatures.
The two orders raise themselves together and proclaim the divine glory.

nasnās.note: Medieval learned and folkloric systems increasingly place the nasnās among jinn.

parī.note: Islamicate Persian translation and folklore sometimes equate jinn with parī.

shiqq.note: Medieval learned and folkloric systems increasingly place the shiqq among jinn.

siʿlāh.note: Medieval learned and folkloric systems increasingly place the siʿlāh among jinn.

sons of God.note: Their unions produce mighty children associated with the Nephilim, although the syntax remains ambiguous.

the Beast.note: Satan’s dragon form grants power and authority to the apocalyptic Beast.

the Elect One.note: They appear in the heavenly liturgy surrounding the Elect One.

the Lamb.myth: The Lamb opens the heavenly seals
the Lamb.note: Revelation portrays Christ as the slaughtered yet living and victorious Lamb.

the Son.note: Milton’s loyal seraphim support the Son’s victory over the rebels.

the Valentinian Savior.myth: The Savior reveals the higher Pleroma
the Valentinian Savior.note: The Savior brings higher knowledge, and the Demiurge eventually learns that powers exist above him.

the abyssal locusts.note: Abaddon is king over the supernatural locust army emerging from the abyss.

the angels.note: The angels prostrate before Adam while Iblīs alone remains defiant.
All angels prostrate at God’s command except Iblīs, who refuses in pride.

the celestial gods.note: The craftsman constructs the celestial gods as components of the ordered living cosmos.

the divine Voice.myth: The arrogant ruler’s boast is rebuked
the divine Voice.note: A divine voice refutes the ruler’s boast and announces an immortal human above him.
the divine Voice.source: Apocryphon of John; Hypostasis of the Archons

the eternal intelligible model.myth: Ordering the cosmos after the eternal model
the eternal intelligible model.note: The craftsman imitates the eternal model when forming the visible cosmos.

the fallen angels.note: Weyer calls Belial the father and seducer of those who fell.

the fallen star.note: The star opens the abyss from which Abaddon's subjects emerge.

the false prophet.note: Satan joins the Beast and false prophet in the lake of fire.

the fifth trumpet angel.note: Abaddon appears during the woe initiated by this angel's trumpet.

the first God.note: Numenius’s second, demiurgic God derives from or depends upon the first God.

the first God.myth: The second God imitates the first
the first God.note: The demiurgic intellect participates in and imitates the first Good.

the four living creatures.note: A wheel accompanies each creature, moving and rising through their shared spirit.

the giants.note: The Watchers father gigantic children with human women.

the good God.note: Marcion’s creator governs this world but stands opposed and inferior to the good God.

the heavenly guards.note: Guards pursue eavesdropping jinn from heaven with fiery projectiles.

the man clothed in linen.note: He enters their wheelwork beneath the Cherubim to receive burning coals.

the sefirot.note: The ten powers are ordered in, represented by, or emanated through Adam Kadmon.

the serpent.myth: The instructor aids knowledge against the ruler
the serpent.note: In some Gnostic rereadings, the serpent promotes knowledge against the ruler, though its identity and evaluation vary.
the serpent.source: Hypostasis; Origin of the World; Ophite reports

the serpent.note: Samael chooses, rides, or inhabits the serpent as his instrument of temptation.
Zoharic passages make Samael the serpent’s ideal or spiritual power.
Christian reception explicitly identifies Satan with the ancient serpent associated with Eden.

the seven angels before God.note: Raphael identifies himself as one of the seven angels standing before God.

the woman clothed with the sun.note: Satan’s dragon pursues the woman and wages war against her offspring.

the world-soul.note: The craftsman mixes, divides, and places the world-soul before and within the cosmic body.

the younger gods.note: The craftsman instructs the younger gods to make mortal creatures while he supplies immortal soul.

the ḥayyot.note: The ḥayyot tremble and acclaim God as Sandalphon's crown ascends.

Ādam.note: Adam appears in the integrated ascent narrative without direct Burāq interaction.

Šāḥar.note: Isaiah calls Hêlēl the shining son of Dawn.

ʿAlī.note: Modern posters juxtapose Burāq with leonine or calligraphic symbols of ʿAlī.

ʿAnanʾel.note: ʿAnanʾel appears with Shemhazai among the oath-bound chiefs of the Watchers.

ʿAzzah.note: ʿAzzah challenges Enoch’s admission to heaven but ultimately acknowledges Metatron’s authority.

ʿAzāʾīl.note: He descends alongside them but repents or withdraws before sharing their sins.

ʿUzzah.note: ʿUzzah challenges Enoch’s admission to heaven but ultimately acknowledges Metatron’s authority.

ʿĪsā.note: Jesus appears in the ascent complex without direct Burāq interaction.

Ṣakhr.note: Comparative tradition equates Ashmedai with Ṣakhr because both steal Solomon's ring and usurp his throne.
